tagline: Southern Portugal's resort coast and barrier-island lagoon — a captive summer market where the islands are reachable only by boat.
summary: The Algarve is southern Portugal's premier resort coast, and the Ria Formosa lagoon behind Faro is a maze of barrier islands — Culatra, Armona, Farol, Deserta — reachable only by water. Marinas at Vilamoura, Albufeira, Lagos and Portimão anchor a dense yachting and resort economy along the coast. Existing island ferries are slow and seasonal; there is no fast, clean, on-demand tier linking the marinas, the barrier islands and the coastal resort towns. It is a captive, high-spend leisure market where the water is the only way to many destinations.
competitive_landscape: Within the Ria Formosa, slow municipal and private ferries serve the barrier islands from Faro and Olhão on limited timetables; along the coast, resort towns are linked mainly by congested summer roads. Nothing offers fast, premium, on-demand water transport across the lagoon and between the marina towns. With island access genuinely water-only and a wealthy seasonal visitor base, a foiling tier serves a captive luxury-and-leisure demand rather than competing for commuters.

demand_signals.label: Ria Formosa barrier islands
demand_signals.note: Culatra, Armona, Farol and Ilha Deserta are reachable only by boat and draw heavy summer day-trip demand on slow ferries — a captive water-only market.

demand_signals.note: The string of resort towns from Lagos to Tavira is linked by congested summer roads paralleling a calm, sheltered coast ideal for fast water hops.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The lagoon-and-coast mesh — Faro↔Culatra/Armona/Farol (~3–4 nm), Olhão↔Deserta (~3 nm), Vilamoura↔Faro (~12 nm), Portimão↔Vilamoura (~18 nm), Lagos↔Portimão (~12 nm) — sits well inside the 70 nm all-electric range. Sheltered lagoon water and short coastal hops suit high-frequency Pioneer II rotations off existing marinas.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: The coastal corridor stays in Pioneer II range; Quanta-LR hybrid range would open longer line-haul east toward the Spanish Costa de la Luz (Faro↔Huelva ~35 nm) or west around Cape St. Vincent without charging dependency.

precedents.why_it_matters: Proves clean foiling networks serving captive, water-only island-resort geographies at scale — the Ria Formosa barrier islands share exactly that access profile.

regulatory_note: The Ria Formosa is a protected Natural Park, strongly favouring zero-emission, low-wash craft over conventional planing boats, and is managed alongside the Portuguese maritime authority and local port administrations. Island ferry concessions and Natural Park permitting are the principal coordination requirements; the protected-lagoon status makes Navier's clean profile a regulatory asset rather than an obstacle.
seasonality: A sharply summer-weighted market (May–October) driven by resort and island-day-trip demand, with a long shoulder season in the Algarve's mild climate; winter activity is thin. The captive island-access role and high-spend visitor base concentrate revenue in the peak months, where reliability and capacity matter most.
